why.core: When you speak, people don't just hear your words. They see your face, your hands and your posture, and they hear your tone, pace and pauses. In a job interview, a presentation or a speech to your council, how you say it can matter as much as what you say. The good news: delivery is a skill you can practise.
why.extend: Oral communication carries meaning beyond the words: eye contact, tone, body language, gesture, pace and intonation shape how an audience receives a message. Controlling these elements, and critically evaluating your own delivery, makes you more credible in interviews, presentations and public debate.

articles.title: It's not just what you say

body.support:
When you talk to a group, people don't just hear your words. They watch your face and body. They hear your voice.

**Eye contact.** Look up from your notes. Look at different people. It shows you're confident.

**Body language.** Stand tall. Keep your feet still. Don't fiddle with a pen. Don't cross your arms.

**Gestures.** Use your hands to help. Open hands look friendly.

**Tone.** Tone is the feeling in your voice. Warm? Serious? Excited? The same words can mean different things.

**Pace and pauses.** Most nervous people talk too fast. Slow down. **Pause** before the most important part.

**Up and down.** Let your voice go up and down. A flat voice sounds bored.

**Mark up your notes.** Use a slash ( / ) for a pause. Underline words to stress. Write “LOOK UP”.

**Nerves are normal.** Breathe out slowly. Practise out loud. Record yourself and watch it back.
body.core:
When you speak to a group, at an interview, in class or at a meeting, your audience takes in much more than your words. They watch your face and body, and they listen to your voice. These are the elements of **oral communication**.

**Eye contact.** Look up from your notes. Look at different people around the room for a second or two each. It shows confidence, and it makes people feel spoken *to*, not *at*.

**Body language.** Stand tall with your weight on both feet. Keep your hands relaxed, not in your pockets or crossed. Swaying, fiddling with a pen or touching your face can make you look nervous, even if you know your stuff.

**Gestures.** Use your hands to add meaning. Open hands invite people in. Counting on your fingers helps people follow a list. Keep gestures natural, and don't overdo them.

**Tone.** Your tone is the feeling in your voice: warm, serious, excited, worried. The same words can mean different things in a different tone.

**Pace and pauses.** Most nervous speakers go too fast. Slow down. **Pause** before your most important point, so people lean in, and after it, so it sinks in.

**Intonation and emphasis.** Let your voice rise and fall. A flat voice sounds bored. Put **emphasis** on key words: *“We need to act **now**.”*

**Plan your delivery.** Mark up your notes: a slash ( / ) for a pause, underline words to stress, “SLOW” where you need to slow down, and “LOOK UP” where you want eye contact.

**Nerves are normal.** Breathe out slowly before you start. Practise out loud, not just in your head. Find a friendly face. And record yourself: watching it back is the fastest way to improve.
body.extend:
Whether you're in an interview, a presentation or a public meeting, your audience receives far more than your words. The **elements of oral communication** (eye contact, body language, gesture, tone, pace and intonation) shape how credible, confident and persuasive you seem.

**Eye contact** signals confidence and connection. Look up from your notes and move your gaze around the room, a second or two per person, so the audience feels addressed.

**Body language** includes posture, stance and facial expression. A balanced, upright stance with relaxed hands projects composure. Swaying, fidgeting or closed postures can signal nerves or defensiveness, even when your content is strong.

**Gesture** reinforces meaning. Open palms invite agreement, and counting on fingers helps an audience track a list. Effective gestures are purposeful and not overused.

**Tone** conveys attitude: warmth, urgency, concern or enthusiasm. The same sentence can carry very different meanings in different tones.

**Pace and pauses** control attention. Nervous speakers tend to rush. A deliberate **pause** before a key point builds anticipation; a pause after lets it land.

**Intonation and emphasis** give speech shape. Rising and falling pitch keeps listeners engaged. Stressing key words directs their focus: *“We need to act **now**.”*

**Planning delivery.** Annotate your notes: a slash for a pause, underlining for emphasis, and cues such as “SLOW” and “LOOK UP”.

**Evaluating yourself.** Recording and reviewing your own delivery is the most reliable way to improve. Watch for specific moments, not just overall impressions.

caseStudies.title: Dylan Alcott takes the stage

body.support:
**Dylan Alcott** is a famous Australian tennis player. He plays wheelchair tennis. In 2021, he won every big title in one year.

In **January 2022**, he was named **Australian of the Year**.

He gave a speech on live TV. He talked about growing up with a disability. He said he wanted to change how people see disability.

Lots of people remembered the speech. Why? It was what he said. It was also how he said it.

Watch the speech. Look for:

- where he looks
- how his voice changes
- where he slows down or stops
- what his face and hands do.

Good speakers practise. You can too.
body.core:
**Dylan Alcott** is one of Australia's best-known athletes. In 2021, he won all four Grand Slam wheelchair tennis titles for quad singles, plus Paralympic gold, in the same year. That's called a **Golden Slam**. He was the first male tennis player ever to do it.

On **25 January 2022**, he was named **Australian of the Year**. Reports at the time said he was the first person with a disability to win the award in its 62-year history.

His acceptance speech was broadcast live across the country. He spoke about growing up with a disability, about how he once felt about himself, and about how he wanted to change things. He said he wanted to change “perceptions so people with disability can live the lives they deserve to live.”

It was a short speech. But people remembered it, and it was shared widely.

Why? Partly because of what he said. But also because of *how* he said it. Watch the speech, and look for:

- where he looks, and who he's talking to
- how his tone changes between serious and funny moments
- where he slows down or pauses
- what his face and hands do.

Great speakers aren't born. They practise, and they make choices about how to say every line.
body.extend:
**Dylan Alcott** is one of Australia's best-known athletes. In 2021, he won the quad wheelchair singles title at all four Grand Slams, and Paralympic gold, in the same year. That's a **Golden Slam**. He was the first male tennis player ever to do it.

On **25 January 2022**, he was named **Australian of the Year**. Reports at the time said he was the first person with a disability to win the award in its 62-year history.

His speech was broadcast live across the nation. He spoke about growing up with a disability, how he once felt about himself, and what he hoped to change. He said his aim was to change “perceptions so people with disability can live the lives they deserve to live.”

The speech was short, but it was widely shared. Its impact came from content and delivery together. In the recording, look at how he uses:

- **eye contact**, to speak to the room and the camera
- shifts in **tone**, between humour and serious moments
- **pace** and **pauses**, to give key lines weight
- his **face** and **hands**, to back up his words.

Powerful delivery is a set of choices. Speakers make them on purpose, and get better through practice.

model.text:
**Topic:** How to change a flat tyre

**My delivery plan**
- **Eye contact:** Look at three people: left, middle and right.
- **Pace:** Slow down for the safety step.
- **Pause:** Two seconds after “Never get under the car.”
- **Intonation:** Voice goes up for the question at the start.
- **Gesture:** Show the turning action for the wheel nuts.

**After watching my recording**
- **Worked:** The pause. It made the safety point stand out.
- **To fix:** I looked at my card too much in the middle.
- **Next time:** Practise once more without the card.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** any four of eye contact, body language, gesture, tone, pace, pauses, intonation, emphasis. Before, so people lean in; after, so it sinks in. Breathe out slowly, practise out loud, find a friendly face, record yourself.

**Script:** 1 eye contact and smile; 2 pause; 3 emphasis on BELIEVED; 4 slow pace; 5 rising then falling intonation; 6 open-hand gesture with the call to action.

**Sort:** looking around — helps; reading every word — hurts; pausing — helps; clicking a pen — hurts; speaking fast — hurts; open hands — helps.

**Same words:** flat and looking away = you don't mean it or don't care; slow, raised eyebrows, rising = sarcasm or doubt; loud, fast, laugh = big, excited praise (or overdone).

**Case study:** answers depend on the viewing; credit specific, observed examples.

realityCheck: **Most students hate watching themselves.** Normalise it, and keep recordings private to the student and you.
**Nervous students need a low-stakes start.** Let them talk to one partner first.
**Pick topics they own.** A talk about their job or sport is easier than a talk about an issue.
**Model the cringe.** Show a recording of yourself and evaluate it out loud.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's the delivery half of Have Your Say.
